authoredPrompt: This figure is a simple colored drawing of a barber pole standing upright on a white ground, annotated with two motion labels. The pole is a tall cylinder capped by an open ellipse, which gives it a three-dimensional read; its curved surface is wrapped by broad helical stripes alternating red, white, blue, and white, tilting downward from left to right and compressing toward the silhouette edges as they turn onto the far side. Above the cylinder, a nearly closed circular arrow drawn in a horizontal plane carries its arrowhead at the upper right, indicating spin about the vertical axis; the words "Real motion" sit above it. To the right, the words "Observed motion" head a short straight arrow pointing vertically downward. Putting a horizontal rotation arrow and a vertical perception arrow in one picture sets the physical direction against the perceived one. The drawing presents the barber-pole display as a case of the aperture problem: the stripes travel around the pole as it turns, yet seen only through the narrow window of the cylinder they register as moving downward.
authoredInteractions:
- Animation for continuously rotating the striped cylinder while an observed-motion arrow updates downward; the stripes wrap around the pole but appear to slide vertically, exposing the aperture-problem mismatch between physical and perceived motion.
- Toggle between real surface motion and observed stripe motion overlays; one view follows points around the cylinder and the other follows the apparent downward bands, making the two motion interpretations separable.
- Slider for stripe angle on the cylinder; the helical bands tilt and the observed-motion arrow changes strength, showing how orientation controls the perceived vertical component.
authoredContext:
The Barber-pole illusion is an illustration of the aperture problem. The barber pole induces the illusion of downward motion while rotating.

### Representation of Optical Flow

discrepancies: stripe density is far lower than the source: the original shows ~6-7 alternating red/blue helical bands wrapping the pole, while the generated texture (repeat=2) shows only ~2 red and ~2 blue bands
the source cylinder has explicit black vertical side outlines framing the silhouette; the generated open-ended cylinder lacks these edge strokes
generated figure adds UI chrome (Pause, overlay toggles, angle slider, status text) not present in the static source
evaluation.notes: A recognizable, pedagogically strong barber-pole aperture illustration with correct primitives, labels, and well-conceived interactions, but the stripe texture has far too few bands compared to the dense red/blue helix of the source.
action_items: Increase the stripe texture repetition (e.g. repeat 3-4 or add more band periods per cycle) so the pole shows many alternating red/blue bands like the source
Add thin black vertical edge lines (or a slightly darker rim shader) along the cylinder silhouette to match the source's outlined sides
Verify the spin-arrow arc direction matches the source's counterclockwise rotation arrow
